question: What is the medical term for an infection of the lower urinary tract involving the bladder?
explanation: Cystitis specifically refers to inflammation and infection of the urinary bladder, typically presenting with dysuria and frequency. [learn more](GNS223_U8_T2#GNS223_U8_T2_h1)

question: Why does passing urine normally help protect your body from infections?

options.A: It physically flushes out bacteria before they can stick to the tract
options.B: It coats the bladder wall with a thick protective mucous layer
options.C: It neutralizes the pH of the urine to stop bacterial growth
options.D: It increases the core body temperature to kill pathogens

explanation: Think of regular urination like a natural tap flush! It sweeps invading germs out of the system before they can settle down and cause trouble.

question: Which common bacterium causes most uncomplicated urinary tract infections?
explanation: E. coli lives happily in our bowels, but when it enters the urinary tract, it becomes the number one culprit behind everyday UTIs!

question: Proteus mirabilis is a type of bacteria strongly linked with which urinary problem?
explanation: Proteus produces a special enzyme that changes urine chemistry, making it easier for painful kidney stones (struvite stones) to form. Good to know in clinical practice!

question: How do fluoroquinolone antibiotics mainly stop bacteria from growing?

options.B: By dissolving the outer bacterial capsule
options.C: By stopping bacterial DNA from copying
options.D: By changing the pH of the blood plasma

explanation: These drugs target the specific machinery bacteria use to copy their genetic material, stopping them right in their tracks.

question: Why is nitrofurantoin great for a simple bladder infection, but not for a deeper kidney infection?

options.A: It is completely destroyed by stomach acid before reaching the bloodstream
options.B: It only kills gram-positive bacteria found exclusively in the urethra
options.C: It concentrates heavily in the urine in the bladder but stays very low in deep kidney tissue
options.D: It requires an acidic environment that only exists in the lower third of the ureters

explanation: Nitrofurantoin travels quickly right into the urine where it hits the bladder hard, but it doesn't build up enough levels in deep tissues to treat kidney infections like pyelonephritis.

question: What is the usual recommended length of time to take nitrofurantoin for a simple bladder infection?
explanation: A short, sweet 5-day course is usually all it takes to clear a simple bladder infection while keeping side effects low.

question: Why is it risky for a patient to stop taking their antibiotics early just because they feel better?

options.A: The kidneys will stop producing urine due to sudden chemical toxicity
options.B: The toughest bacteria can survive, multiply, and cause a stronger, drug-resistant infection
options.C: The patient will permanently lose their normal bowel flora
options.D: The body will develop an immediate allergy to that specific drug class

explanation: Stopping early leaves behind the strongest germs. They bounce back stronger and won't respond to the same medicine next time!

question: Which of these makes a urinary tract infection automatically classified as 'complicated'?

options.A: The patient is a non-pregnant adult female
options.B: The infection occurs in a male patient
options.C: Urinalysis shows trace amounts of blood
options.D: Symptoms started less than 24 hours ago

explanation: Because of male anatomy and possible prostate involvement, any UTI in a male is automatically treated as complicated.

question: Why are urine cultures a must-have when managing a complicated urinary tract infection?

options.A: Complicated infections involve tougher, varied bacteria that need specific, targeted drugs
options.B: Rapid dipstick tests are completely illegal to use in complicated hospital cases
options.C: Cultures prove to the hospital administration that the nurse followed proper protocol
options.D: Laboratories require a culture sample before they will dispense any antibiotic medication

explanation: Complicated UTIs can be stubborn and caused by unusual germs. A culture helps us find the exact right antibiotic so the patient heals faster.

question: What is the standard first-line injection used to treat uncomplicated gonorrhea?
explanation: Ceftriaxone as a single injection is our go-to treatment because older drugs unfortunately don't work well anymore due to resistance.

question: Why is azithromycin or doxycycline often given along with ceftriaxone for a gonorrhea patient?

options.A: To boost the pain-relieving effect of ceftriaxone
options.B: To neutralize the acidic pH of the reproductive tract
options.C: To cover a common co-infection with chlamydia
options.D: To prevent the patient from developing a fungal yeast infection

explanation: Gonorrhea and chlamydia love to travel together! Giving dual therapy ensures we knock out both sneaky infections at the same time.

question: What is a major cause of high antibiotic resistance rates in our communities?

options.A: Drinking too much clean municipal water
options.B: Eating fresh fruits and locally grown vegetables
options.C: Buying drugs over-the-counter and not finishing the full dose
options.D: Performing routine urinalysis testing too frequently

explanation: Self-medicating and stopping courses halfway trains bacteria to survive drugs, creating superbugs that are hard to treat.

question: What happens when bacteria become resistant to older, cheaper antibiotics?

options.A: Doctors have to switch to more expensive or stronger alternative drugs
options.B: Pharmacies stop stocking antibacterial medications altogether
options.C: Patients require fewer laboratory tests before starting therapy
options.D: Infections disappear faster because bacteria become weaker over time

explanation: When cheap first-line drugs fail, patients face higher costs and sometimes harsher treatments. That's why fighting resistance is so crucial!

question: When should you collect a midstream urine sample for a lab culture if the patient needs antibiotics?

options.A: On the final day of the antibiotic course
options.C: It does not matter when the sample is collected
options.D: Before giving the very first dose of antibiotic

explanation: Always collect the sample first! If you start antibiotics before taking the sample, the drug will kill the bacteria in the lab dish and give you a false negative result.

question: A patient says her urine smells strong and asks for leftover antibiotics from a friend. As her nurse, what should you tell her?

options.A: Advise her to mix the leftover pills with water to make a soothing wash
options.B: Explain that taking leftover drugs without a proper prescription can cause treatment failure and drug resistance
options.C: Tell her she can use half the dose her friend took since her symptoms are milder
options.D: Confirm that sharing antibiotics is a safe and affordable way to save money on clinic fees

explanation: Great nurses educate with empathy! Gently guide patients away from sharing medications and encourage them to visit the clinic for the right diagnosis.
